Question: How do I train for a 5k run, if I'm used to running longer distances and have never been in a race?
Old_Answer: Start doing a HIIT (high intensity interval training) routine 2 or 3 days a week. It's really simple. I use a 8/12 second cycle. Basically, I do an easy jog for 5 minutes. Then 20 minutes of 8 seconds of all out sprint alternating with 12 seconds slow trot (60 cycles). Then I end with a 5 minute cool down trot followed by stretching. The stretching is vital to prevent injury. The HIIT routine will boost your VO2 max allowing your muscles to perform longer and stronger. On the other days you run, have a metronome with you. You can download one for free on a smartphone or buy a tiny one cheap from most music stores. Figure out what your general foot cadence is. Get the metronome beat to match your steps. Once you figure out your current pace, start bumping it up 3-5 beats per minute each time you run. This will speed up your pace like you won't believe. Good luck!

Start by incorporating speed work into your routine—intervals or tempo runs can help you adapt. For instance, you could do 400-meter repeats at a pace that's faster than your goal race pace, allowing ample recovery in between. Secondly, consider adding a few race-specific workouts that mimic the 5k distance but at a slightly slower pace than your goal time. This will build familiarity with the distance while keeping your longer runs in your weekly schedule, which will help maintain your endurance. Lastly, don’t forget to practice running at race pace during your training. You can also simulate race conditions by participating in local 5k events or time trials, which can help acclimate you to the competitive atmosphere. Remember, while you're used to longer distances, a 5k is a different beast—embrace the challenge and enjoy the process. And as the race day approaches, taper your mileage to ensure you're fresh and ready to go; this is a sprint, not a marathon!

Old_Answer: My paternal grandfather had a catalog of around 50 boogie woogie piano songs in his head. My grandmother, on the other hand, took piano lessons for many years. She could play virtually anything that you put in front of her. If she was accompanying a singer and they were having trouble hitting the high notes, she could transpose into a lower key on the fly. Both of my grandparents spent around the same amount of time learning the piano.
